title: Federal Court Blocks Key Asylum Fee Penalties Under One Big Beautiful Bill Act
excerpt: A Massachusetts district court has temporarily stayed USCIS from rejecting asylum applications or terminating work permits over unpaid annual asylum fees, offering relief to TPS holders and pending asylum applicants.
body:
• A U.S. District Court in Massachusetts on July 21, 2026, issued an administrative stay blocking USCIS from enforcing several H.R. 1 provisions that penalized asylum applicants and TPS beneficiaries for unpaid fees.
  • The court order prevents USCIS from rejecting asylum applications, terminating work authorization, or initiating removal proceedings solely over failure to pay the Annual Asylum Fee (AAF).
  • TPS-based Employment Authorization Documents (EADs) that were previously extended will retain their original expiration dates, rather than being cut short under the new rules.
  • USCIS may still collect the AAF, and all other H.R. 1 immigration fee requirements remain in effect pending further litigation.

What the Court Ordered

The U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts granted an emergency motion for an administrative stay on July 21, 2026, in the case Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts, et al. v. United States Citizenship and Immigration Services, et al. (Case No. 26-cv-13038-NMG). The plaintiffs — membership-based organizations representing TPS holders and pending asylum applicants — argued that several USCIS enforcement actions under H.R. 1, the Reconciliation Act of 2025 (widely known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act), would cause irreparable harm to their members.

https://x.com/MassDailyNews/status/2082794846486425742

The court agreed in part, staying four specific enforcement actions that USCIS had begun implementing through a July 2025 Federal Register Notice, a March 2026 website update, and an April 2026 Interim Final Rule (IFR).

According to USCIS's own announcement, the agency "will comply with the court's order pending further judicial proceedings."

The Four Provisions on Hold

The stay covers significant ground. First, USCIS cannot apply H.R. 1's new rules to TPS-based Employment Authorization Document expiration deadlines. Any TPS-based EAD that had been previously extended will maintain its prior expiration date, rather than being shortened to one year or the remaining TPS designation period — a cap the April 2026 IFR had imposed.

Second, the court blocked USCIS from rejecting asylum applications solely because applicants failed to pay the Annual Asylum Fee within 30 days of notification. Under the IFR that took effect May 29, 2026, non-payment triggered automatic rejection of a pending Form I-589 asylum application.

Third, USCIS cannot terminate work authorization as a consequence of AAF non-payment. The IFR had stipulated that applicants who received an Employment Authorization Document based on a pending asylum application would lose that work permit immediately upon rejection.

Fourth, the court barred USCIS from initiating removal proceedings based solely on an applicant's failure to pay the AAF — a provision that had raised alarm among immigration advocates as one of the harshest consequences in the new fee structure.

Background: The Annual Asylum Fee

The AAF was created by H.R. 1, signed into law on July 4, 2025. USCIS published its initial implementing notice on July 22, 2025, establishing a filing fee for asylum applications (Form I-589) and an annual fee payable each calendar year an application remains pending. The fee started at $100 and rose to $102 on January 1, 2026, according to immigration law site Nolo. No fee waiver is available for low-income applicants.

On April 28, 2026, DHS announced the interim final rule that gave the fee its teeth: non-payment within 30 days of notification would result in rejection of the asylum application, denial of any pending work authorization request, immediate loss of existing work permits, and — for those without other legal status — the initiation of removal proceedings.

"The interim final rule establishes that if an alien does not pay the AAF within 30 days of notification, USCIS will reject their pending asylum application. If an alien does not have legal status in the U.S., USCIS will also initiate the alien's removal."

— USCIS announcement, April 28, 2026

Impact on Indian Immigrants

While the lawsuit was brought by organizations primarily representing Venezuelan and other Latin American TPS holders, the court order applies broadly. Indian nationals with pending asylum applications — a growing category given increased asylum filings from India in recent years — stand to benefit from the stay. Those who had been scrambling to pay the AAF under threat of application rejection and deportation now have temporary breathing room.

For Indian TPS holders, though the number is smaller compared to other nationalities, the EAD expiration date protection is significant. Many rely on work authorization to maintain employment in the U.S., and a sudden shortening of EAD validity periods could have caused immediate job disruptions.

The ruling also lands in the context of broader immigration litigation. In a separate case in June 2026, a federal judge in Rhode Island struck down USCIS policies that had paused immigration benefit adjudications for nationals of 39 countries, finding them rooted in "anti-immigrant sentiments," according to Reuters. India was among the countries affected by some of these broader holds on benefit processing.

What Remains in Effect

The court's order is narrow in one important respect: USCIS may still collect the Annual Asylum Fee. Anyone who has received or receives a notice regarding the AAF must still pay according to the instructions in that notice, according to the USCIS alert. All other fees and requirements under H.R. 1, including the Form I-589 filing fee and the Form I-102 fee, continue in full effect.

The stay is temporary and contingent on further judicial proceedings. USCIS said it "will provide updated instructions as further litigation developments occur."

What to Watch

The Massachusetts case is still in its early stages. The court granted an administrative stay — not a preliminary injunction — meaning a more substantive ruling on the merits could come in the weeks ahead. Whether the government appeals or seeks to narrow the order will shape how long these protections last.

Immigration attorneys are watching whether this case follows the trajectory of other recent court challenges to H.R. 1 implementation, which have generally found USCIS overstepping its authority. For now, asylum applicants and TPS holders can rely on the stay to prevent the most severe consequences of non-payment — but they should still pay the AAF to remain in compliance with the portions of the law that the court left intact.
nri_angle: Indian asylum applicants and TPS holders benefit from the court stay that prevents USCIS from rejecting applications or terminating work permits over unpaid annual asylum fees.
